html:
A Japanese tea master, the most important single figure in the history of the tea ceremony.

He was born to a merchant family in Sakai, the rich trading port near Osaka. He studied tea from youth and served as tea master first to Oda Nobunaga and then to Toyotomi Hideyoshi, the warlords who united Japan.

Rikyū pushed tea toward wabi: a beauty of the plain, worn and imperfect. He built tiny tea rooms, some only two mats in size, with a low door that made every guest, lord or merchant, crawl in as equals. He favoured rough local Raku bowls over costly Chinese wares. Much of what tea means in Japan, including its ideas of hospitality and calm, goes back to him.

Being so close to Hideyoshi also made him a political player. In 1591, for reasons still debated, Hideyoshi ordered him to kill himself, and he did. Three houses of his descendants, the Urasenke, Omotesenke and Mushakōjisenke, still teach his way of tea.
sum: A Japanese tea master, the most important single figure in the history of the tea ceremony.
